result.question: I need to know whether the fault in Transformer 1 at MAIN is getting worse or changing character. Run a DGA fault classification on the first and the last complete oil sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Tell me each sample's fault class and confidence. Then tell me whether the class moved toward a higher-energy or higher-temperature fault, for example PD to D1, or T1 to T2/T3. If the two classifications disagree, explain which one you trust more and why, based on the absolute gas levels and not just the ratios. Then recommend one specific next check, such as a confirmatory resample, an OLTC compartment sample or an electrical test. Count a sample as complete only if all five gases are non-null. If there is only one complete sample in the window, classify that one alone and say that no progression can be judged.
result.answer:
Retried both; the DGA interpretation tool is persistently unavailable ("LLM unavailable"). I have all five gases for every sample, so I computed the IEC 60599 Rogers Ratios directly rather than leave you without an answer. Please note the classification below is my manual calculation, not the tool's output.

**Samples used (all five gases non-null in all 4 rows; first = 2024-01-15, last = 2024-01-18)**

| | H2 | CH4 | C2H6 | C2H4 | C2H2 | R1 C2H2/C2H4 | R2 CH4/H2 | R3 C2H4/C2H6 | IEC code |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2024-01-15 | 2845 | 7406 | 5467 | 16684 | 7 | 0.0004 | 2.60 | 3.05 | 0-2-2 |
| 2024-01-18 | 2900 | 7350 | 5450 | 16600 | 7 | 0.0004 | 2.53 | 3.05 | 0-2-2 |

**Fault class and confidence**
- 2024-01-15: **T3 – thermal fault >700 °C** (Rogers code 0-2-2). Confidence: high that it is a thermal hot-metal fault (R1 ≈ 0 and R2 > 1 are unambiguous); moderate on T3 vs T2, because R3 = 3.05 sits right on the Rogers boundary (>3) and below the stricter IEC 60599 T3 limit (>4).
- 2024-01-18: **T3 – thermal fault >700 °C** (Rogers code 0-2-2). Same confidence and same caveat.

**Progression**
No change in character. Both samples give the identical code and essentially identical ratios (all ratios moved <3%). The class did not move toward a higher-energy fault: acetylene stayed at ~7 ppm (0.04% of ethylene), so there is no drift toward D1/D2 arcing, and R3 did not climb further into T3 territory. The two classifications agree, so there is no disagreement to adjudicate.

**What the absolute levels say (the more important story)**
The ratios are stable, but the concentrations are extreme: C2H4 ≈ 16,600 ppm, CH4 ≈ 7,400, C2H6 ≈ 5,450, H2 ≈ 2,900. These are roughly 50–100× IEC 60599 typical 90th-percentile values and far beyond IEEE C57.104 Condition 4. The 4-day flatness (±2%) should not be read as "fault inactive": at these levels the oil is likely near gas saturation and may be off-gassing to the conservator/headspace, which masks the generation rate. The near-absence of acetylene is the one reassuring point — this is severe overheating of metal, not arcing, and it also makes OLTC-compartment contamination of the main tank unlikely (OLTC leakage would normally bring acetylene with it).

**Recommended next check (one)**
De-energized DC winding-resistance test on all three phases across every tap position, with a core-to-ground insulation resistance check during the same outage. A resample would only reconfirm four already-consistent results, and an OLTC sample is not indicated given ~0 acetylene; the winding-resistance/core-ground test is the direct way to locate the hot-metal source (bad joint, tap-lead connection, or circulating core current) driving >16,000 ppm ethylene. Given the severity, this should be scheduled as an urgent outage rather than a routine one.
